file: papers/pdf/Pease et al - 2013 - A Discussion on Serendipity in Creative Systems.pdf
about: The paper analyses serendipitous discovery in humans (prepared mind, trigger, bridge, result; chance, sagacity, value; focus-shift; environmental factors) and proposes a definition and standards for computational serendipity, evaluating three creative systems.

candidates.label: Happy accidental unsought discovery
candidates.definition: A serendipitous discovery is one where chance plays a crucial role and which yields a surprising, often unsought, useful finding such as a product, idea or artefact.
candidates.applies_when: An account describes finding something useful by accident that was not being looked for, with chance playing a key part.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The finding was planned and reached through deliberate design with no chance element.

candidates.label: Pseudoserendipity (sought finding)
candidates.definition: A discovery that was being sought but whose solution arises from an unknown, unlikely, coincidental or unexpected source.
candidates.applies_when: The person was actively pursuing a goal or problem and the answer came from an unexpected or coincidental source.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The finding was not sought at all (true serendipity in Walpole's sense).

candidates.label: Focus-shift / re-evaluation
candidates.definition: A radical change in what the discoverer judges interesting: something previously seen as a mistake, nuisance, refuse, irrelevant or unimportant is re-evaluated as interesting; the original focus may be abandoned or pursued alongside.
candidates.applies_when: Someone describes coming to see a failure, side effect, discarded item, accident or nuisance as valuable or worth pursuing.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Problem reformulation that re-represents a problem rather than re-evaluating an example or artefact as interesting.

candidates.label: Prepared mind
candidates.definition: The discoverer's previous experiences, background knowledge, store of unsolved problems, skills and current focus, on which a discovery draws.
candidates.applies_when: An account links recognising the opportunity to prior experience, expertise, skills or open problems the person was already carrying.

candidates.label: Serendipity trigger
candidates.definition: The event or item arising immediately before the discovery, such as a dream, an anomalous observation, burs on a jacket, or discarded failed material.
candidates.applies_when: A specific unexpected observation, object, event or encounter is identified as what set the discovery off.

candidates.label: Bridging reasoning
candidates.definition: Techniques that take the discoverer from trigger to result, notably abduction (explaining a surprising observation), analogical reasoning (transferring from a source domain), and conceptual blending.
candidates.applies_when: The person explains how they reasoned from an odd observation to an idea, e.g. explaining an anomaly, drawing an analogy to another domain, or combining ideas.

candidates.label: Chance dimension
candidates.definition: The trigger is unlikely, unexpected, unsought, accidental, random, surprising or coincidental, arising independently of and before the result.
candidates.applies_when: The account emphasises luck, coincidence, accident or surprise in how the trigger arose.

candidates.label: Sagacity dimension
candidates.definition: The skill of the discoverer: an open mind to exploit the unpredictable, ability to shift focus, suitable reasoning, and ability to recognise value; others in the same position often failed to make the discovery.
candidates.applies_when: The person stresses their own ability to notice, be open to, or see the value of something others overlooked.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Mere chance with no skilled recognition; the author says serendipity is not 'mere chance'.

candidates.label: Value dimension
candidates.definition: The result must be happy and useful, evaluated externally; discoveries need not score high on every dimension.
candidates.applies_when: The accidental finding is described as useful or beneficial, judged by others or the market.

candidates.label: New product, process or use
candidates.definition: The result of serendipity may be a new product, artefact, process, hypothesis, or a new use for an object.
candidates.applies_when: The serendipitous episode yields a new product, process or application (e.g. a side effect becoming the main use).

candidates.label: Dynamic world
candidates.definition: Data arriving in stages rather than as a complete, consistent whole makes serendipity more likely.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes operating amid changing, streaming or incrementally arriving information when the discovery happened.

candidates.label: Multiple contexts
candidates.definition: Information from one domain being used in another facilitates serendipitous discovery.
candidates.applies_when: The account describes carrying knowledge or an idea across from a different field or context.

candidates.label: Multiple tasks
candidates.definition: Discoverers were often engaged in several tasks at once, which favours serendipity.
candidates.applies_when: The person was juggling several projects or activities when the discovery occurred.

candidates.label: Social context / other people
candidates.definition: Discoveries take place in a social context and the unexpected source is sometimes another person, e.g. recalling a colleague's failed glue.
candidates.applies_when: An account credits a colleague, conversation or other person as the source of the unexpected input.

candidates.label: Negative serendipity / derailment
candidates.definition: The same traits that aid serendipity can lead to being derailed from the task, a surprising fact not being properly investigated, or a discovery prevented by chance interruptions.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes an unexpected observation that was misread or not pursued, or a distraction that cost progress.

candidates.label: Tension with systematic focus
candidates.definition: There is tension between systematicity and serendipity; openness to chance may inhibit producing desired results, and a focused heuristic approach may perform better.
candidates.applies_when: An account weighs staying focused on a plan against exploring chance leads.

candidates.label: Retrospective serendipity framing
candidates.definition: Because serendipity is romantic and value-laden, people framing work for the public may tell a serendipity backstory, which can over- or under-rate its role and may even be fictional.
candidates.applies_when: The person narrates a luck/accident origin story, especially for public audiences, or downplays luck to emphasise own merit.

candidates.label: Little-s vs Big-S serendipity
candidates.definition: Everyday, mundane serendipity distinguished from ground-breaking, domain-changing serendipitous discoveries.
candidates.applies_when: Coders can distinguish minor everyday lucky finds from major field-changing ones in the account.

candidates.label: Serendipity skills can be taught
candidates.definition: Serendipity-facilitating skills can be taught; much writing on serendipity aims to teach others the skills involved, and environments can raise the likelihood of chance discoveries.
candidates.applies_when: A person describes deliberately cultivating openness or arranging circumstances to increase chance encounters.
